clue.text: National symbol of course next to bridge

indicators.note: next to places the golf links side by side with the following piece

parts.note: St Andrews in Fife is the most famous golf course in Scotland
to bridge a river is to cross it

explanation.surface: An emblem of the country stands on a golf links beside a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' is the Old Course at St Andrews, the Scottish home of golf, and 'bridge' is a verb. 'next to' simply sets the two side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: The saltire, a white diagonal on blue, is Scotland's flag and so an emblem of that nation.

clue.text: New ally close to the Pope, not the clergy

indicators.note: new tells you the letters that follow are to be put in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter, here taken from the next word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A recent friend who has the pontiff's ear turns out not to be a priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges ALLY, E and POPE together; the E is the last letter of 'the', picked by 'close to'. The fodder runs unbroken through the middle of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The laity are the members of a church who are not ordained, the opposite group to priests.

clue.text: Most of boxing rings I judge small but stylish

indicators.note: as a verb, to ring is to encircle, so the fight word goes round the two letters
most of a word is all but its final letter, so the last one is dropped

parts.note: a bout is a boxing match
J is the abbreviation for judge, as in a court title

explanation.surface: A ringside official rates most of the fighting arenas as compact but chic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rings' looks like a noun going with boxing but is the verb: BOU (BOUT cut short by 'Most of') goes round I and J.
explanation.definitionFit: Estate agents' favourite adjective for a property that is compact yet elegant, borrowed from the French for jewel.

clue.text: WWI battle scene keeping old exhibits behind

indicators.note: keeping means the place name holds the letter inside it

parts.note: Mons in Belgium was the site of the first British battle of the First World War in 1914

explanation.surface: A battlefield from the Great War still holds its historic displays at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' is a noun, not a position: the definition is the verb phrase for baring the buttocks. 'keeping' puts O inside MONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang verb: someone who bares their buttocks at others as a prank or insult does this.

clue.text: The best alternative on our menu

indicators.note: alternative suggests another version of the letters that follow, a different arrangement of them

parts.note: taken as written, nine letters

explanation.surface: A restaurant boasts that the finest choice of dish is on its list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternative' asks for another arrangement of ON OUR MENU.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from Italian or Spanish for number one, an idiom for the top person or thing.

clue.text: One in denial moreover's always right

parts.note: nay is an old word for moreover or indeed, as in 'good, nay excellent'; the possessive supplies the S
aye is a Scots and poetic word for always or ever

explanation.surface: Somebody who refuses to accept the facts is, on top of that, never wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Two archaic words do the work: NAY for 'moreover' (with the 's attached) and AYE for 'always'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who habitually says no, contradicting or refusing whatever is proposed.

clue.text: Fish, for example, being out of this world, makes impression

parts.note: the Fish, Pisces, is one sign of the zodiac
ET, an extraterrestrial, is a creature from beyond the earth

explanation.surface: A fish dish, say, is so heavenly that it wows the diners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being' is a noun, a creature, and 'out of this world' is literal. 'makes' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a small seal and also the mark such a seal stamps in wax.

clue.text: Whisk you need for eggnog

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to whisk someone away is to carry them off quickly and secretly
eggnog is made with eggs, milk and a strong alcoholic drink such as rum or brandy

explanation.surface: A recipe names the utensil required to make a Christmas drink.
explanation.definitionFit: One verb sense, to carry off swiftly, and one noun sense, strong distilled liquor, share the word.

clue.text: Bachelor circles repeatedly with lass in dance

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in BA

indicators.note: in, at the end of the phrase, says the girl sits inside the run of round letters
repeatedly asks for the pair of round letters to be written a second time

parts.note: circles in the plural are a pair of round letters, O and O
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A single man twirls round and round with a girl on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circles' is a noun for the round letter: a pair, doubled by 'repeatedly', makes four, and 'with lass in' splits them two and two around the girl. The second 'in' is not needed; the one after 'lass' does the inserting.
explanation.definitionFit: A 1960s Latin-influenced soul style of dancing from New York, so an example of the category.

clue.text: Lent money? You won't have to wait for it

definitions.text: You won't have to wait for it

parts.note: Lent is the forty-day Christian period of abstinence before Easter, a fast
a buck is slang for a dollar, and so for cash generally

explanation.surface: A loan is on offer with the cash handed over on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lent' is the season, not the past tense of lend. The whole clue also hints at the answer: money made quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for easy profit made quickly, so cash that arrives without delay.

clue.text: History repeating itself, democracy clearly shows

indicators.note: shows says the two words display the answer within their run of letters

explanation.surface: Popular government plainly demonstrates that the past comes round again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' tells you the answer sits inside 'democracy clearly', spanning the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A series of events that recurs in the same order is exactly the past coming round again.

clue.text: Diners out usually book table, first of all making reservation

indicators.note: first of all asks for the opening letter of each of the five words before it

explanation.surface: People eating at a restaurant generally phone ahead to secure a table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first of all' takes the opening letters of the five words before it; 'making' links to the definition, which is a misgiving rather than a booking.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of a misgiving: to have reservations about a plan is to be unsure of it.

clue.text: Equipped with large leg — like a hare?

indicators.note: with joins the kitted-out word to the two short pieces, which the answer puts first

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
in cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side
geared, as in geared up, means fitted out with kit

explanation.surface: An animal has a big hind limb, much as a hare does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leg' is cricket: the leg side of the pitch, to the batsman's left if right-handed, is also called the ON side. 'with' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A hare is a typical example of an animal with lengthy lugs, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Rocket propelling circus performer towards drum?

definitions.meaning: in British slang a rocket is a sharp telling-off
a whimsical picture: the tiny insect star of a miniature circus sent into the part of the head that holds a drum

explanation.surface: A firework launches a big-top artiste at a percussion instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a stinging rebuke; taken literally it puts a tiny jumping insect by somebody's eardrum.

clue.text: Distant country looms after switching on one's lights

indicators.note: switching means changing the positions of the letters of the word before it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
one is I, and with the possessive S gives IS
to light is to come down and settle, as a bird alights

explanation.surface: A faraway nation comes into view once somebody turns on the lamps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lights' is a verb, to come down and settle, not lamps; 'after switching' rearranges only the word before it, and the surface's 'on' and 'one's' are used almost as they stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pacific archipelago state east of Papua New Guinea, far from Britain.

clue.text: Possible description of the UN for people in general

parts.note: the article that starts the three-word description
NY is New York, where the United Nations has its headquarters
a body is an organisation, which the United Nations is

explanation.surface: Someone offers a way of summing up the United Nations for ordinary folk.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into three: the UN, based in Manhattan, could be called 'a New York organisation', using the city's two-letter abbreviation. 'for' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pronoun for any person at all, whoever they may be.

clue.text: Arrange lecture with no publicity

indicators.note: with no says the publicity word is absent from the lecture word

parts.note: an address is a formal speech or lecture
an ad is a piece of advertising

explanation.surface: Someone organises a talk but does nothing to promote it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes one AD from ADDRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrange a shop window, hair or a salad is to prepare and set it out neatly.

clue.text: Daughter, say, upset after old joke gets deleted

indicators.note: after puts the turned pair of pieces behind the old joke

parts.note: ex means former, as in an ex-partner
a pun is a joke that plays on words

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means overturned, so the pair before it is read from the bottom up

parts.note: D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter
eg means for example, or say

explanation.surface: A girl, for instance, is distressed when a stale gag is cut from the script.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' overturns two pieces at once, giving GED, and 'after' sends that to the foot of the answer. 'gets' links to the definition, so nobody is actually distressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: something struck out or erased from a record has been removed completely.

clue.text: Blue, like bathroom mirrors sometimes?

definitions.meaning: blue describes films or jokes that are sexually explicit
after a hot shower a bathroom mirror mists over with condensation

explanation.surface: The glass in the washroom occasionally takes on an azure tint.
explanation.definitionFit: One adjective covers both erotic content and a surface fogged with water vapour.

clue.text: Again hiding from soldiers in rugby ground

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

indicators.note: ground is the past tense of grind, so the letters before it are crushed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Somebody conceals themselves from the troops once more at a rugby stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' is not a stadium but the anagram signal, rearranging IN RUGBY into BURYING. 'from' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting something back under the earth is concealing it a second time.

clue.text: Turned to embrace girl on noon visit

indicators.note: in a down clue on means on top of, so what precedes sits above the final letter
to embrace is to hold in the arms, so the first word wraps round the name

parts.note: milk that has turned has gone sour
Jo is a girl's name, short for Josephine or Joanne

explanation.surface: Someone spins round to hug a young woman who has called in at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' wants to be a reversal signal; it is a description of milk gone off. 'to embrace' and 'on' do the building, the latter in its down-clue sense of sitting above.
explanation.definitionFit: A temporary stay somewhere, a synonym as noun or verb.

clue.text: Vexed young child, one who cancels invite to do

parts.note: someone put out is annoyed or offended
a tot is a toddler
to cancel something is to end it, so the person doing so is an ender

explanation.surface: An annoyed toddler is the kind who calls off an invitation to a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a party but is the verb: the definition means to ask firms to bid to carry out a job.
explanation.definitionFit: Business idiom for asking contractors to submit bids to carry out a piece of work.

clue.text: Philosopher with noble title forgoing it

indicators.note: with adds the shortened word after the noble one

parts.note: aristo is an informal short form of aristocrat

indicators.note: forgoing means giving up, so the word before it loses the two letters named after

explanation.surface: A thinker of high birth gives up his peerage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forgoing' takes IT out of TITLE, leaving TLE, which 'with' attaches to ARISTO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek thinker, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great, is an example.

clue.text: Room where one can go with family to study

indicators.note: with joins the family word on after the room

parts.note: loo is British for the toilet, and to go is a euphemism for using it
kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: A den in the house where a person can retreat with relatives to read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go' is the lavatorial euphemism: LOO is the everyday British word for a toilet. 'with' joins KIN, and TO is as written.
explanation.definitionFit: To investigate or examine a matter, a synonym as a verb.

clue.text: One prophet failing to finish folios, sulking

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: failing to finish means the name stops short of its final letter

parts.note: Nahum is one of the minor prophets of the Old Testament
ff is the abbreviation for folios, the plural of f

explanation.surface: A seer who could not complete his manuscript pages is in a mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing to finish' drops the last letter of NAHUM, a minor Old Testament prophet.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for being in a fit of petty bad temper, as a moody person is.

clue.text: By chance, mostly, Irish lake becomes Swiss one

definitions.note: one stands for lake, so a lake in Switzerland

indicators.note: mostly means the word before it is used without its final letter

parts.note: luck is chance or fortune
Lough Erne is a pair of lakes in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Through sheer fortune, more or less, a lough in Ireland turns into an Alpine one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims LUCK to LUC. 'By' places it beside ERNE, and 'becomes' links to the definition, where 'one' means a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A lake in central Switzerland, with a city of the same name on its shore.

clue.text: Most important bits involved in clue

indicators.note: involved can mean tangled or complicated, so the letters after it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The key parts of the puzzle are wrapped up in one hint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' means tangled here: it rearranges IN CLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: The central cores of atoms, cells or groups, round which the rest gathers.

clue.text: Town boasted ultimate in lifestyle

parts.note: crew is a past tense of crow, to brag

indicators.note: the ultimate letter in a word is its final one

explanation.surface: A place bragged that it offered the very best way of living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimate in' picks the last letter of 'lifestyle'. CREW is the older past tense of crow, to brag.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway junction in Cheshire, in north-west England, is an example.
